name: Battle of Kosovo
info: An Ottoman army under Sultan Murad I fought an army led by the Serbian Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović on the Kosovo field in 1389; both leaders died, both armies were badly weakened, and the Serbian principalities later became Ottoman vassals.

facts.date: 15 June 1389; Vidovdan, the day the battle is commemorated, falls on 28 June in the Gregorian calendar, and a Florentine letter of 20 October 1389 gives 28 June (St Vitus' day)
facts.place: The Kosovo field, about 5 kilometres north-west of Pristina, in present-day Kosovo, on land ruled by Vuk Branković
facts.sides: The Ottoman Empire under Sultan Murad I, leading estimate 27,000 to 30,000 men, with a higher estimate of 40,000; a coalition under Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović, leading estimate 15,000 to 20,000, with a higher estimate of 25,000. Both figures are disputed.
facts.outcome: Lazar and Murad were both killed and most of both armies were lost. Serbian manpower was depleted, and the Serbian principalities that were not already Ottoman vassals became so in the following years.

t: No account by a participant survives, and the earliest reports differ so much that the course of the battle cannot be reconstructed with confidence; estimates of the armies run from 15,000 to 20,000 for Lazar and 27,000 to 30,000 for Murad.
Murad I was killed, the only time an Ottoman sultan died in battle, and tradition ascribes his death to the Serbian knight Miloš Obilić, though early accounts differ on who killed him and when.

The Kosovo Myth, built on motifs of sacrifice, betrayal and heroism, grew from oral epic poetry and gained its modern importance in the 19th century, and Vidovdan is now an important Serbian national and religious holiday.
dyk: The battle is the only time in history an Ottoman sultan was killed in battle, yet a Florentine letter of 1389 names no killer, and an Italian work of 1416 says that Lazar killed Murad.
ev: The Ottomans destroy much of the Serbian nobility at the Battle of Maritsa, and Stefan Uroš V dies childless in December
The Ottomans are defeated at Pločnik, and again at Bileća in 1388
Murad I moves his troops from Philippoupolis to Ihtiman and on towards Kosovo
Murad arrives at Pristina on 14 June and Lazar brings his army to the Kosovo field
The battle is fought on 15 June, and Murad and Lazar are both killed
Tvrtko I of Bosnia writes to Trogir and Florence claiming a victory over the Ottomans
The Ottomans renew their campaign in southern Serbia, 1390 to 1391
The capture of Smederevo on 20 June ends medieval Serbian statehood

sections.background:
Stefan Uroš IV Dušan, who ruled from 1331 to 1355, was succeeded by his son Stefan Uroš V, whose reign saw the decline of central power and the rise of many virtually independent principalities. This period is known as the fall of the Serbian Empire. Uroš V could neither keep the empire his father had made nor repel foreign threats, and he died childless in December 1371, after much of the Serbian nobility had been destroyed by the Ottomans at the Battle of Maritsa earlier that year.

Prince Lazar, ruler of the northern part of the former empire, known as Moravian Serbia, was aware of the Ottoman threat and began diplomatic and military preparations against the Ottomans. After Ottoman defeats at Pločnik in 1386 and Bileća in 1388, the sultan Murad I moved his troops from Philippoupolis to Ihtiman in the spring of 1388, and on through Velbužd and Kratovo. The route was longer than the alternative through Sofia and the Nišava Valley, but it led to Kosovo, one of the most important crossroads in the Balkans, from which Murad could attack the lands of either Lazar or Vuk Branković.

Murad marched through Kumanovo, Preševo and Gjilan to Pristina, where he arrived on 14 June. Less is known of Lazar's preparations. He gathered his troops near Niš and, once he learned that Murad had moved to Velbužd, went across Prokuplje to Kosovo, a place that gave him control of all the routes Murad could take.
sections.forces:
The composition of both armies is a matter of scholarly dispute, and no reliable information exists. The battle was nonetheless one of the largest of the late Middle Ages. It is generally believed that the Ottoman army was larger. The leading estimate accepted by Western scholars gives Lazar 15,000 to 20,000 troops and Murad 27,000 to 30,000; a higher estimate suggests 40,000 Ottomans and 25,000 for Lazar's coalition. The Ottoman historian Mehmed Neşri, writing in 1521, put the Christian coalition at around 500,000, double the Ottoman army; Noel Malcolm holds that Ottoman writers exaggerated it.

The Ottoman army was reinforced by Muslim vassals and allies from Anatolia, among them auxiliaries from the Beylik of Isfendiyar. It comprised no more than 2,000 Janissaries and as many as 8,500 cavalrymen, and it probably included the forces of two Serbian rulers who were Ottoman vassals, Marko Kraljević and Konstantin Dejanović. Murad led the centre, his son Bayezid and the commander Evrenoz the European troops on the right wing, and his son Yakub the Anatolian troops on the left. About 1,000 archers fortified the wings, and the Janissaries held the centre.

Lazar's coalition was mainly his own Serbian contingent, troops of his son-in-law Vuk Branković, and Bosnians under Vlatko Vuković sent by King Tvrtko I. Lazar led the centre, Branković the right and Vuković the left, which also held the foreign contingents. Albanians, Croatians, Hungarians, Vlachs and Bulgarians are said to have joined, but Dejan Djokić later judged a broad coalition improbable.
sections.course:
Serbian and Turkish accounts differ, which makes the course of events hard to reconstruct. It is believed that the battle began with Ottoman archers shooting at the Serbian cavalry, who then prepared to attack. Formed in a wedge, the Serbian cavalry broke through the Ottoman left wing, which Yakub Çelebi commanded, but did less well against the centre and the right wing.

After the knights' charge was spent, light Ottoman cavalry and light infantry counterattacked, and the Serbian heavy armour became a disadvantage. In the centre the Serbs pushed back the Ottomans, except for Bayezid's wing, which barely held off the Bosnians under Vuković, who inflicted disproportionately heavy losses on it. Bayezid then led a fierce counterattack that pushed the Serbian forces back, and the Ottomans routed the Serbian infantry later in the day.

Vuk Branković is said to have left the field when he saw there was no hope of victory, after Lazar had been captured, in order to save as many men as he could. Oral tradition calls this a betrayal, a view first set out by Mavro Orbini in 1601 and largely seen as unfounded. The remaining Bosnian and Serbian forces then yielded the field. In one of the earliest accounts twelve knights broke through the Ottoman defence, and one of them, later identified as Miloš Obilić, feigned desertion and killed Murad with a hidden dagger before the sultan's bodyguards killed him. Another version has Obilić playing dead and stabbing Murad as he walked past. Sources also differ on whether this came early in the battle or after it had turned.
sections.aftermath:
Both armies were largely destroyed, and both Lazar and Murad lost their lives. Murad's son Bayezid, hearing of his father's death, killed his younger brother Yakub Çelebi and became the sole heir to the throne. The Serbs were left with too few men to defend their lands effectively, while the Ottomans had many more troops in the east. Hungary tried to exploit the depletion of Serbian manpower by expanding in northern Serbia, and the Ottomans renewed their campaign in southern Serbia as early as 1390 to 1391.

The Serbian feudal class split in two. A northern faction favoured a conciliatory, pro-Ottoman policy as a defence against Hungary, and a southern faction, directly threatened by Ottoman expansion, looked to Hungary. Some principalities that were not already vassals became so, and their lords, among them Lazar's daughter, formed marriage ties with Bayezid. Lazar's son Stefan Lazarević became a loyal ally of Bayezid and contributed forces to his later campaigns, including the Battle of Nicopolis. Branković had joined the anti-Ottoman coalition there, and Lazarević was rewarded with a large part of his lands. Branković died an Ottoman prisoner.

The news spread quickly in Europe, and early rumours dwelt on the death of the sultan. Tvrtko of Bosnia wrote to the senate of Trogir on 1 August and to the council of Florence claiming a victory over the Ottomans. Over the following decades Serbia formally became an Ottoman province, and the capture of Smederevo on 20 June 1459 marks the end of medieval Serbian statehood.
sections.sources:
No first-hand account by a participant exists. The contemporary sources come from widely diverging points of view, and they say little about tactics, army sizes or the field. European reports of the time were mostly concerned with the death of Murad and a supposed Christian victory. The earliest Serbian sources owe more to religious rhetoric than to historical data. Every contemporary account was composed under religious, political and literary influences, and scholars can only try to trace the early strands of tradition that later became part of the Kosovo Myth.

The Florentine reply to Tvrtko of 20 October 1389 confirms that Murad was killed and that the battle took place on 28 June, St Vitus' day. It does not name the killer, but praises twelve loyal lords who cut their way to Murad's tent through a circle of chained camels, and the one who stabbed the sultan. Mignanelli's work of 1416 says Lazar killed him. The first detailed Ottoman account is Neşri's, which exaggerates the size of Lazar's army and describes the battle as a significant Ottoman victory.

Who fought is disputed. Albanian historiography stresses the Albanian share, which on its reading of Ottoman sources may have been a quarter of Lazar's coalition, while Serbian historiography minimises or ignores it; the presence of Teodor II Muzaka is verified, that of Đurađ II Balšić contested. Obilić may rest on a Hungarian knight, a claim modern scholars take seriously. Daniel Waley holds that next to nothing can be said with assurance about the numbers and multi-ethnic make-up of either army.
sections.legacy:
The Kosovo Myth has long been central to Serbian folklore and literature, kept for centuries mainly in oral epic poetry and the songs of the guslars. It began soon after the event and grew from different originators into various versions. In the 19th century Vuk Karadžić collected the epic poems of the Kosovo cycle, which became the final version of the myth. Its modern telling rests on sacrifice (Lazar choosing a heavenly kingdom over an earthly one), betrayal (Branković's supposed desertion) and heroism (Obilić's killing of Murad).

Miodrag Popović notes that in Ottoman Serbia in the 16th and 17th centuries the local population was Turkophilic, in a climate of adaptation to Ottoman rule, and did not read the legend as hostile to the Ottomans. Serbian historiography came to simplify the political setting into a clash between Christianity and Islam. Perceptions changed with Serbian nationalism in the 19th century; for most of it the Principality of Serbia saw Bosnia, not Kosovo, as its core. The Congress of Berlin in 1878 handed Bosnia to Austria-Hungary, leaving Kosovo as the only route for Serbian expansion, and this raised the Kosovo Myth to its modern status.

Vidovdan, celebrated on the Julian calendar, is an important part of Serb national identity. Events on that day include Serbia's declaration of war on the Ottoman Empire in 1876, the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914, the Vidovdan Constitution of 1921 and Slobodan Milošević's Gazimestan speech in 1989. Albanian epic songs in Kosovo also tell of the battle, centred on Obilić, called Millosh Kopiliqi.

summary: On the Kosovo field in 1389 an Ottoman army under Murad I fought a coalition under the Serbian Prince Lazar. Both leaders died and both armies were largely destroyed. Little reliable detail survives, but the battle has been central to Serbian memory, and Vidovdan commemorates it.
references: Thomas Allan Emmert, Serbian Golgotha: Kosovo, 1389 (East European Monographs, 1990)
Rade Mihaljčić, The Battle of Kosovo in history and in popular tradition (Beogradski izdavačko-grafički zavod, 1989)
N. Malcolm, Kosovo: A Short History (Macmillan, 1998)
John V. A. Fine, The Late Medieval Balkans: A Critical Survey from the Late Twelfth Century to the Ottoman Conquest (University of Michigan Press, 1994)
notes: Date: the article's lead and span say 15 June 1389; the Florentine letter and Vidovdan give 28 June (St Vitus' day), which the article treats as the Julian/Gregorian difference in the modern era only. Both given in facts; the article does not reconcile them.
Source discrepancy: the article gives Neşri's Ottoman account as 1521 in one place and 1512 in another; I wrote 1521 (army size) and left the other out of the sources section.
The article says Lazar was 'captured' in the Branković passage, and the lead says Lazar was killed; it does not say how or when Lazar died. I wrote only 'both Lazar and Murad lost their lives'.

Left out as garbled: 'Mehmed's death in 1421 ... future Mehmed the Conqueror' (the article's Mehmed seems to be confused); the line 'Murad's army consisted of no more than 2,000 Janissaries ... Murad's army comprised' is run together in the article but its figures are kept.
'Historical facts say' Branković fled to save men: the article's phrase is hedged by the next sentence; I attributed it as the article's view with 'is said to have'.
The article says Ottoman sources claim camels placed in front; the Florentine letter also names chained camels; I used the letter only.
